name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q01 - Definition of inheritance and variation in genetics

questiontext.text: In genetics, the process by which characters are passed on from parent to progeny, and the degree by which progeny differ from their parents, are respectively termed:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Genetics is the branch of biology that deals with the inheritance as well as the variation of characters from parents to offspring.

Step 2: Evaluation
Inheritance is defined as the process by which characters are passed on from parent to progeny and forms the basis of heredity. Variation is defined as the degree by which progeny differ from their parents.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The two terms in respective order are inheritance and variation.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q02 - Development of Sahiwal cows by artificial selection

questiontext.text: Well-known Indian cattle breeds such as Sahiwal cows in Punjab were developed from ancestral wild cows primarily through:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Early humans recognised that sexual reproduction generates variation and exploited naturally occurring variations in wild populations.

Step 2: Evaluation
Through selective breeding, artificial selection, and domestication from ancestral wild cows, organisms possessing desirable characters were chosen to produce breeds such as Sahiwal cows in Punjab.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Sahiwal cows were developed through artificial selection and domestication.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q03 - Number of true-breeding pea varieties selected by Mendel

questiontext.text: During his seven-year hybridisation experiments (\(1856\text{–}1863\)) on garden peas, how many true-breeding pea plant varieties did Gregor Mendel select?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mendel conducted artificial pollination experiments on garden pea using pairs of lines that differed in one contrasting character.

Step 2: Evaluation
Mendel studied \(7\) characters, each having \(2\) contrasting traits (dominant and recessive), making a total of \(14\) true-breeding pea plant varieties.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Mendel selected \(14\) true-breeding pea plant varieties.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q04 - Characteristic feature of a true-breeding pea line

questiontext.text: A true-breeding line in Mendel's experiments is one that:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
True-breeding lines are homozygous for the character under study, ensuring uniform gametes and consistent trait expression.

Step 2: Evaluation
Having undergone continuous self-pollination, a true-breeding line shows stable trait inheritance and expression for several generations without segregation of contrasting traits.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A true-breeding line undergoes continuous self-pollination and shows stable trait inheritance and expression for several generations.

answer.text: Is always heterozygous for the trait under observation
Produces two distinct types of gametes in equal proportions
Undergoes continuous self-pollination and shows stable trait inheritance for several generations

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q05 - Identifying recessive traits in garden pea

questiontext.text: Which of the following is a recessive trait among the seven characters studied by Mendel in Pisum sativum?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In Mendel's seven pairs of contrasting traits in garden pea, one trait is dominant and expressed in \(F_1\), while the other is recessive.

Step 2: Evaluation
Axial flower position, green pod colour, and round seed shape are all dominant traits. By contrast, yellow pod colour is the recessive trait (green pod colour is dominant).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Yellow pod colour is the recessive trait.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q06 - Phenotypic and genotypic ratios in monohybrid F2 generation

questiontext.text: When Mendel self-pollinated the tall \(F_1\) pea plants (\(Tt\)) obtained from a cross between true-breeding tall (\(TT\)) and dwarf (\(tt\)) parents, the \(F_2\) phenotypic and genotypic ratios were, respectively:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The \(F_1\) heterozygote has genotype \(Tt\) and is self-pollinated (\(Tt \times Tt\)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
\(T\) (tall) is completely dominant over \(t\) (dwarf).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
According to the Law of Segregation, \(Tt\) produces gametes \(T\) and \(t\) in equal proportions (\(\frac{1}{2}\) each).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Random fertilisation yields \(\frac{1}{4}\,TT : \frac{1}{2}\,Tt : \frac{1}{4}\,tt\), which is a genotypic ratio of \(1:2:1\). Since both \(TT\) and \(Tt\) appear tall, \(\frac{3}{4}\) of the progeny are tall and \(\frac{1}{4}\) are dwarf, giving a phenotypic ratio of \(3:1\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The sum of fractions equals \(1\). The phenotypic and genotypic ratios are \(3:1\) and \(1:2:1\), respectively.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q07 - Incomplete dominance in snapdragon flower colour

questiontext.text: In snapdragon (Antirrhinum sp.), when a true-breeding red-flowered plant (\(RR\)) is crossed with a true-breeding white-flowered plant (\(rr\)), the \(F_1\) progeny bear pink flowers. This phenomenon is an example of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When the \(F_1\) heterozygote exhibits an intermediate phenotype that does not resemble either homozygous parent, the allele interaction is called incomplete dominance.

Step 2: Evaluation
In Antirrhinum sp., \(R\) is not completely dominant over \(r\), so the \(Rr\) heterozygote produces pink flowers instead of red or white.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The phenomenon is incomplete dominance.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q08 - Total genotypes and phenotypes in human ABO blood groups

questiontext.text: In the human population, the ABO blood group system is controlled by three alleles (\(I^A\), \(I^B\), and \(i\)). How many total genotypes and phenotypes are possible for ABO blood groups in humans?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Humans are diploid organisms, so each individual carries two alleles of the \(I\) gene. With three alleles in the population, multiple allelic combinations are possible.

Step 2: Evaluation
The six possible genotypes are \(I^A I^A\), \(I^A i\), \(I^B I^B\), \(I^B i\), \(I^A I^B\), and \(ii\). These produce four distinct phenotypes: blood group A (\(I^A I^A, I^A i\)), blood group B (\(I^B I^B, I^B i\)), blood group AB (\(I^A I^B\)), and blood group O (\(ii\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
There are \(6\) genotypes and \(4\) phenotypes.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q09 - Suitability of Drosophila melanogaster for Morgan's experiments

questiontext.text: Which of the following is not a reason why Thomas Hunt Morgan selected Drosophila melanogaster for verifying the chromosomal theory of inheritance?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Morgan chose Drosophila melanogaster because it has practical experimental advantages for genetic crosses.

Step 2: Evaluation
Drosophila can be grown on simple synthetic medium, completes its life cycle in about two weeks, produces a large number of progeny from a single mating, shows clear sexual dimorphism, and has hereditary variations visible under low-power microscopes. It does not require a long generation time of several years; rather, its short life cycle of about two weeks made it ideal.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Completing its life cycle in several years is not a reason for selecting Drosophila melanogaster.

answer.text: It completes its life cycle in several years, allowing slow observation
It can be grown on simple synthetic medium in the laboratory
A single mating produces a large number of progeny flies
Male and female flies are easily distinguishable

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q10 - Chromosomal basis of Down's syndrome

questiontext.text: Down's syndrome in humans is caused by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Down's syndrome is an autosomal aneuploidy first described by Langdon Down in \(1866\).

Step 2: Evaluation
It results from the presence of an additional copy of chromosome \(21\) (trisomy of chromosome \(21\)), bringing the total chromosome number to \(47\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Down's syndrome is caused by trisomy of chromosome \(21\).

answer.text: Presence of an additional copy of chromosome \(21\) (trisomy of \(21\))
Presence of an additional X chromosome (\(47, XXY\))
A single base substitution in the \(\beta\)-globin gene

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q11 - Postulates of Mendel's Law of Dominance

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements accurately summarises Mendel's Law of Dominance?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mendel proposed the Law of Dominance based on his monohybrid cross observations, where only one parental trait appeared in \(F_1\) and both reappeared in a \(3:1\) ratio in \(F_2\).

Step 2: Evaluation
The three postulates of the Law of Dominance are: (i) characters are controlled by discrete units called factors, (ii) factors occur in pairs, and (iii) in a dissimilar pair of factors, one member dominates (dominant) the other (recessive).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Characters are controlled by discrete paired factors, and in a dissimilar pair, one factor dominates the other.

answer.text: Alleles of a pair blend in the \(F_1\) hybrid to produce an intermediate phenotype
Factors of different characters always assort together into the same gamete
Characters are controlled by discrete paired factors, and in a dissimilar pair one dominates the other
A gamete always receives both members of a factor pair during meiosis

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q12 - Evidence and mechanism of Mendel's Law of Segregation

questiontext.text: The recovery of the recessive parental trait in the \(F_2\) generation without any blending provides direct evidence for:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Law of Segregation states that alleles do not blend in a heterozygote and separate during gamete formation so each gamete receives only one allele.

Step 2: Evaluation
Even though the recessive allele is masked in the \(F_1\) generation, it remains unchanged and segregates cleanly into \(50\%\) of the gametes during meiosis, allowing homozygous recessive individuals to reappear intact in \(F_2\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
This demonstrates the Law of Segregation.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q13 - Binomial expansion of monohybrid F2 genotypic ratio

questiontext.text: In a monohybrid cross where \(F_1\) heterozygotes (\(Tt\)) are self-pollinated, the \(F_2\) genotypic ratio \(\frac{1}{4}\,TT : \frac{1}{2}\,Tt : \frac{1}{4}\,tt\) can be mathematically represented by expanding which binomial expression?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The \(F_1\) plant has genotype \(Tt\) and produces gametes \(T\) and \(t\) in equal frequency (\(\frac{1}{2}\) each).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Random fertilisation combines male and female gamete probabilities independently.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The binomial expansion \((ax + by)^2\) models the union of two gamete pools each with frequencies \(a = \frac{1}{2}\) for \(T\) and \(b = \frac{1}{2}\) for \(t\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Expanding \(\left(\frac{1}{2}T + \frac{1}{2}t\right)^2 = \left(\frac{1}{2}T + \frac{1}{2}t\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}T + \frac{1}{2}t\right) = \frac{1}{4}TT + \frac{1}{2}Tt + \frac{1}{4}tt\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The coefficients \(\frac{1}{4}, \frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{4}\) sum to \(1\) and match the \(1:2:1\) genotypic ratio. The correct expression is \(\left(\frac{1}{2}T + \frac{1}{2}t\right)^2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q14 - Purpose and outcome of a Mendelian test cross

questiontext.text: To determine whether a violet-flowered pea plant (dominant phenotype) has genotype \(WW\) or \(Ww\), it is crossed with a white-flowered plant (\(ww\)). If the progeny consist of \(50\%\) violet-flowered and \(50\%\) white-flowered plants, the unknown parent is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
An organism with a dominant phenotype (violet flower, unknown genotype \(WW\) or \(Ww\)) is crossed with a homozygous recessive parent (\(ww\), white flower). The progeny are \(50\%\) violet and \(50\%\) white.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
\(W\) is dominant over \(w\). The white-flowered parent (\(ww\)) produces only \(w\) gametes.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
In a test cross, the phenotypic ratio of offspring directly reflects the gametic ratio of the tested dominant-phenotype parent.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
If the unknown parent were homozygous dominant (\(WW\)), it would produce only \(W\) gametes, yielding \(100\%\) \(Ww\) (all violet) offspring. Since \(50\%\) of the offspring are white (\(ww\)), the unknown parent must have contributed \(w\) gametes as well as \(W\) gametes in equal proportion, meaning its genotype is heterozygous \(Ww\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Crossing \(Ww \times ww\) gives \(1\,Ww\text{ (violet)} : 1\,ww\text{ (white)}\), matching the \(50\%:50\%\) observation. Thus, the unknown parent is heterozygous (\(Ww\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q15 - Biochemical explanation of dominant and recessive alleles

questiontext.text: Suppose an unmodified allele produces a normal enzyme required to convert substrate \(S\) into a product. Under what condition will a modified allele generally behave as a recessive allele?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Dominance arises from the functional sufficiency of the unmodified allele in a heterozygote.

Step 2: Evaluation
If a modified allele produces a normal or equally efficient enzyme, it is equivalent to the unmodified allele and produces the same phenotype. However, if the modified allele produces a non-functional enzyme or no enzyme at all, the phenotype in a heterozygote depends solely on the functioning unmodified allele; hence the unmodified allele is dominant and the modified allele is recessive.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A modified allele generally behaves as recessive when it produces a non-functional enzyme or no enzyme at all.

answer.text: When it produces an enzyme with normal efficiency
When it produces a non-functional enzyme or no enzyme at all
When it is located on a non-homologous chromosome

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q16 - Co-dominance in human ABO blood group alleles

questiontext.text: Why do individuals with the genotype \(I^A I^B\) have blood group AB?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In co-dominance, the \(F_1\) or heterozygous individual resembles both parents because both alleles express their respective gene products simultaneously.

Step 2: Evaluation
Alleles \(I^A\) and \(I^B\) produce slightly different forms of sugar polymers on the plasma membrane of red blood cells, whereas allele \(i\) produces no sugar. When \(I^A\) and \(I^B\) are present together in \(I^A I^B\), both express their own types of sugars on the red blood cell surface.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both \(I^A\) and \(I^B\) express their own types of sugars simultaneously due to co-dominance.

answer.text: \(I^A\) is incompletely dominant over \(I^B\), forming an intermediate sugar
Neither \(I^A\) nor \(I^B\) produces any sugar on the red blood cell surface
Both \(I^A\) and \(I^B\) express their own types of sugars simultaneously due to co-dominance

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q17 - Starch grain size versus seed shape dominance in pea

questiontext.text: In garden pea, starch synthesis is controlled by a single gene with alleles \(B\) and \(b\). Heterozygous \(Bb\) plants produce round seeds but starch grains of intermediate size. What does this illustrate about dominance?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A single gene product can influence more than one phenotype, and the apparent dominance relationship depends on which phenotype is examined.

Step 2: Evaluation
For seed shape, \(BB\) and \(Bb\) both produce round seeds while \(bb\) produces wrinkled seeds, making \(B\) appear completely dominant over \(b\). However, for starch grain size, \(BB\) produces large grains, \(bb\) produces small grains, and \(Bb\) produces intermediate-sized grains, showing incomplete dominance.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Dominance is not an autonomous feature of a gene; it depends on the gene product and the specific phenotype chosen for examination.

answer.text: Dominance is not an autonomous feature of a gene and depends on the phenotype examined
Seed shape and starch grain size are controlled by two unlinked genes
Allele \(b\) is completely dominant over allele \(B\) for starch synthesis
Starch synthesis in pea seeds is a polygenic trait

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q18 - Gamete types and frequencies in dihybrid RrYy plant

questiontext.text: According to Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment, an \(F_1\) dihybrid pea plant with genotype \(RrYy\) produces which four types of gametes, and in what frequency?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The \(F_1\) dihybrid genotype is \(RrYy\), where \(R/r\) and \(Y/y\) assort independently.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
\(50\%\) of gametes receive \(R\) and \(50\%\) receive \(r\); independently, \(50\%\) receive \(Y\) and \(50\%\) receive \(y\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By the Law of Independent Assortment, the probability of each combined gamete is the product of the individual allele probabilities.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Each of the four combinations \(RY\), \(Ry\), \(rY\), and \(ry\) has a probability of \(\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{4}\), which equals \(25\%\) of the total gametes produced.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(4 \times 25\% = 100\%\). The four gamete types are \(RY, Ry, rY, ry\), each at \(25\%\) frequency.

answer.text: \(RY\) and \(ry\) at \(40\%\) each; \(Ry\) and \(rY\) at \(10\%\) each

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q19 - Derivation of dihybrid 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio

questiontext.text: In Mendel's dihybrid cross between round yellow (\(RRYY\)) and wrinkled green (\(rryy\)) pea plants, the \(F_2\) phenotypic ratio \(9:3:3:1\) can be derived mathematically as a combination series of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Two independently assorting characters are studied: seed shape (round vs wrinkled) and seed colour (yellow vs green).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
In \(F_2\), each character individually segregates in a \(3:1\) dominant-to-recessive phenotypic ratio.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Independent assortment means the combined phenotypic distribution is the product of the two monohybrid ratios.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\((3\text{ Round} : 1\text{ Wrinkled}) \times (3\text{ Yellow} : 1\text{ Green}) = 9\text{ Round, Yellow} : 3\text{ Round, Green} : 3\text{ Wrinkled, Yellow} : 1\text{ Wrinkled, Green}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(9 + 3 + 3 + 1 = 16\), matching the \(16\) squares of the dihybrid Punnett square. The combination series is \((3\text{ Round} : 1\text{ Wrinkled})(3\text{ Yellow} : 1\text{ Green})\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q20 - Reasons Mendel's work remained unrecognised until 1900

questiontext.text: Which of the following was not a reason why Mendel's work on inheritance remained unrecognised from \(1865\) until \(1900\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mendel published his work in \(1865\), but it was overlooked by contemporaries for several historical and scientific reasons.

Step 2: Evaluation
Communication was difficult so his work was not widely publicised; his concept of discrete, non-blending factors was rejected as an explanation for continuous variation in nature; his mathematical approach to biology was unfamiliar and unacceptable to many biologists; and he could not provide physical proof for the existence or composition of factors. By contrast, his experiments did not have a small sample size—they actually had a large sampling size that gave his data high credibility.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Having a small sampling size was not a reason, as Mendel used a large sampling size.

answer.text: Communication was limited and his work could not be widely publicised
His mathematical approach to biological phenomena was unacceptable to many biologists
He could not provide physical proof for the existence or nature of factors
His experiments had a very small sampling size, making his data unreliable

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q21 - Scientists who independently rediscovered Mendel's laws in 1900

questiontext.text: In \(1900\), Mendel's results on the inheritance of characters were independently rediscovered by which trio of scientists?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
At the turn of the twentieth century, three European botanists independently arrived at the same laws of inheritance that Mendel had published in \(1865\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns, and Erich von Tschermak independently rediscovered Mendel's results in \(1900\). Sutton and Boveri later formulated the chromosomal theory of inheritance in \(1902\), while Morgan and Sturtevant worked on linkage and gene mapping in Drosophila.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The three scientists were de Vries, Correns, and von Tschermak.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q22 - Parallelism in chromosomal theory of inheritance

questiontext.text: Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri proposed the chromosomal theory of inheritance based on the observation that:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sutton and Boveri united cytological knowledge of chromosome movement during meiosis with Mendelian principles of inheritance.

Step 2: Evaluation
Both chromosomes and genes occur in pairs, segregate at the time of gamete formation so that only one of each pair enters a gamete, and independent pairs segregate independently of one another. Thus, the behaviour of chromosomes during meiosis parallels the behaviour of Mendelian factors (genes).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The behaviour of chromosomes during meiosis is parallel to the behaviour of genes.

answer.text: Chromosomes occur singly in somatic cells and duplicate only after fertilisation
The behaviour of chromosomes during meiosis is parallel to the behaviour of genes
Genes are located in the cytoplasm and assort independently of the nucleus
Homologous chromosomes never separate during reduction division

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q23 - Morgan's concept of linkage and recombination

questiontext.text: In Morgan's dihybrid crosses on Drosophila involving two sex-linked genes located on the X chromosome, the \(F_2\) ratio deviated significantly from \(9:3:3:1\) because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mendel's \(9:3:3:1\) dihybrid ratio requires the two genes to assort independently, which occurs when they are on different chromosomes or far apart.

Step 2: Evaluation
When two genes are situated on the same chromosome, they are physically associated (linked). Consequently, the proportion of parental gene combinations in the progeny is much higher than that of non-parental (recombinant) combinations.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Physical association (linkage) of the two genes on the same chromosome resulted in a much higher proportion of parental combinations than non-parental types.

answer.text: Non-parental combinations were produced in much higher proportion than parental combinations
The two genes were located on different autosomes and showed incomplete dominance
The two genes were physically linked on the same chromosome, yielding more parental combinations
Male Drosophila flies do not transmit their X chromosome to any progeny

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q24 - Recombination frequency and genetic mapping by Sturtevant

questiontext.text: In Drosophila, Morgan found \(1.3\%\) recombination between the genes for yellow body (\(y\)) and white eye (\(w\)), and \(37.2\%\) recombination between white eye (\(w\)) and miniature wing (\(m\)). Based on Alfred Sturtevant's genetic mapping principle, this indicates that:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Alfred Sturtevant used the frequency of recombination between gene pairs on the same chromosome as a measure of the physical distance between them.

Step 2: Evaluation
A lower recombination frequency (\(1.3\%\) for \(y\) and \(w\)) means the genes are very tightly linked and located close together on the chromosome. A higher recombination frequency (\(37.2\%\) for \(w\) and \(m\)) means the genes are loosely linked and located farther apart.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Genes \(y\) and \(w\) are more tightly linked and closer together on the chromosome than genes \(w\) and \(m\).

answer.text: Genes \(w\) and \(m\) are closer together on the chromosome than \(y\) and \(w\)
Genes \(y\) and \(w\) are located on different chromosomes
Strength of linkage is directly proportional to recombination frequency
Genes \(y\) and \(w\) are more tightly linked and closer together than \(w\) and \(m\)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q25 - Additive allelic effect in polygenic human skin colour

questiontext.text: In polygenic inheritance of human skin colour controlled by three genes (\(A, B, C\)), where dominant alleles contribute to dark colour and recessive alleles to light colour, an individual with three dominant alleles and three recessive alleles (e.g., \(AaBbCc\)) will have:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a polygenic trait, the phenotype reflects the additive contribution of each allele, and traits are spread across a continuous gradient.

Step 2: Evaluation
The genotype \(AABBCC\) (six dominant alleles) produces the darkest skin colour, and \(aabbcc\) (six recessive alleles) produces the lightest skin colour. A genotype with three dominant alleles and three recessive alleles (\(AaBbCc\)) has an equal balance of both and therefore exhibits an intermediate skin colour.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The individual will have an intermediate skin colour.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q26 - Pleiotropy illustrated by phenylketonuria

questiontext.text: Phenylketonuria is cited as an example of pleiotropy because a single mutation in the gene coding for the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase results in:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A pleiotropic gene is a single gene that exhibits multiple phenotypic expressions, typically by affecting a metabolic pathway that contributes to several traits.

Step 2: Evaluation
In phenylketonuria, a single-gene mutation affecting phenylalanine hydroxylase manifests phenotypically as mental retardation as well as a reduction in hair and skin pigmentation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The single mutation results in both mental retardation and reduced hair and skin pigmentation.

answer.text: Only mental retardation without any external physical changes
Both mental retardation and a reduction in hair and skin pigmentation
Sickling of red blood cells and defective blood clotting
Failure to distinguish between red and green colours

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q27 - Female heterogamety in birds versus male heterogamety

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes sex determination in birds from that in humans and grasshoppers?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sex-determining mechanisms are classified as male heterogamety or female heterogamety depending on which sex produces two distinct types of gametes with respect to sex chromosomes.

Step 2: Evaluation
In humans (\(XY\) males, \(XX\) females) and grasshoppers (\(XO\) males, \(XX\) females), males are heterogametic. In contrast, birds exhibit female heterogamety: females have one \(Z\) and one \(W\) chromosome (\(ZW\)), producing two types of eggs, whereas males are homogametic (\(ZZ\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
In birds, females are heterogametic (\(ZW\)) and males are homogametic (\(ZZ\)), whereas in humans and grasshoppers, males are heterogametic.

answer.text: In birds, males are heterogametic (\(ZW\)) and females are homogametic (\(ZZ\))
In birds, females have fewer total chromosomes than males
In birds, females are heterogametic (\(ZW\)) and males are homogametic (\(ZZ\))
In grasshoppers, females are heterogametic (\(XO\)) and males are homogametic (\(XX\))

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q28 - Sex determination by sperm in human beings

questiontext.text: In human beings, what is the probability of having a female child in each pregnancy, and which parent's gamete determines the sex of the child?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Humans have \(22\) pairs of autosomes and \(1\) pair of sex chromosomes (\(XX\) in females, \(XY\) in males).

Step 2: Evaluation
Females produce only one type of ovum carrying an X chromosome. Males produce two types of sperm in equal proportions: \(50\%\) carry an X chromosome and \(50\%\) carry a Y chromosome. Fertilisation of an X-bearing ovum by an X-bearing sperm produces a female (\(XX\)), while fertilisation by a Y-bearing sperm produces a male (\(XY\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
There is a \(50\%\) probability of a female child in each pregnancy, and the genetic makeup of the sperm (father's gamete) determines the sex.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q29 - Haplodiploid sex determination features in honey bee

questiontext.text: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of the haplodiploid sex-determination system in honey bees?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In honey bees, females are diploid (\(32\) chromosomes) and develop from fertilised eggs, whereas males (drones) are haploid (\(16\) chromosomes) and develop from unfertilised eggs by parthenogenesis.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because males are haploid, they produce sperm by mitosis rather than meiosis. Furthermore, since males arise from unfertilised eggs, they do not have a father and cannot have sons, though they have a grandfather and can have grandsons.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Male honey bees are haploid, produce sperm by mitosis, and have no father.

answer.text: Males are haploid (\(16\) chromosomes), produce sperm by mitosis, and do not have a father
Females are haploid (\(16\) chromosomes) and develop from unfertilised eggs
Males are diploid (\(32\) chromosomes) and produce sperm by meiosis
Unfertilised eggs always develop into diploid worker females

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q30 - Types of DNA mutations and mutagens

questiontext.text: Deletions or insertions of base pairs of DNA cause ______, whereas a change in a single base pair of DNA is known as ______.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mutations alter DNA sequences and consequently change the genotype and phenotype of an organism.

Step 2: Evaluation
Deletions and insertions of base pairs shift the reading frame of the genetic code and are therefore called frame-shift mutations. A change in a single base pair of DNA (such as in sickle-cell anaemia) is called a point mutation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The two terms in order are frame-shift mutations and point mutation.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q31 - Sex-linked recessive inheritance of colour blindness

questiontext.text: Red-green colour blindness occurs in about \(8\%\) of males but only about \(0.4\%\) of females because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Red-green colour blindness is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by a mutation in genes on the X chromosome affecting red or green cone cells of the eye.

Step 2: Evaluation
Males have only one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele on that X chromosome expresses the disorder. Females have two X chromosomes, so a recessive allele on one X chromosome is masked by a dominant normal allele on the other; a female expresses colour blindness only when homozygous recessive (inheriting the mutant allele from both a carrier/affected mother and an affected father).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Males have only one X chromosome while females have two X chromosomes, making expression of an X-linked recessive trait much more frequent in males.

answer.text: The gene for colour blindness is located on the Y chromosome
It is an autosomal dominant trait with higher penetrance in males
It is an X-linked recessive trait, and males have only one X chromosome while females have two
Females lack cone cells in the retina required for red-green discrimination

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q32 - Haemophilia inheritance and Queen Victoria pedigree

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements about haemophilia is incorrect?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Haemophilia is an X-linked recessive disorder in which a single protein of the blood clotting cascade is affected, leading to non-stop bleeding from simple cuts.

Step 2: Evaluation
An unaffected heterozygous carrier female (such as Queen Victoria) can transmit the mutant allele to her sons. However, a female becoming haemophilic is extremely rare because her mother must be at least a carrier and her father must be haemophilic (who is often unviable in the later stage of life). Therefore, claiming that a haemophilic female can be born to a normal father is incorrect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A female becoming haemophilic does require a haemophilic father, so the statement that she can be born to a normal father is incorrect.

answer.text: It is a sex-linked recessive disease transmitted from carrier females to male progeny
A single protein involved in the cascade of blood clotting is affected
Queen Victoria was a carrier of the disease and had several haemophilic descendants
A female can commonly become haemophilic even if her father is completely normal

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q33 - Metabolic accumulation in phenylketonuria

questiontext.text: In phenylketonuria, the accumulated phenylalanine is converted into ______ and other derivatives, whose accumulation in the brain causes mental retardation and which are excreted in urine due to ______.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Phenylketonuria is an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism caused by lack of the enzyme that converts phenylalanine into tyrosine.

Step 2: Evaluation
In the absence of this enzyme, phenylalanine accumulates and is converted into phenylpyruvic acid and other derivatives. Accumulation of these substances in the brain causes mental retardation, and they are also excreted through urine because of poor absorption by the kidney.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The missing phrases are phenylpyruvic acid and poor absorption by the kidney.

answer.text: phenylpyruvic acid; poor absorption by the kidney
phenylpyruvic acid; active secretion by the liver

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q34 - Comparing Klinefelter's syndrome and Turner's syndrome

questiontext.text: Compare Klinefelter's syndrome and Turner's syndrome: individuals with Klinefelter's syndrome have a karyotype of ______ and show ______, whereas individuals with Turner's syndrome have a karyotype of ______ and have ______.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Both Klinefelter's syndrome and Turner's syndrome are sex-chromosomal aneuploidies resulting in sterility.

Step 2: Evaluation
Klinefelter's syndrome is caused by an additional X chromosome, giving a karyotype of \(47, XXY\); such individuals have overall masculine development with gynaecomastia (development of breasts) and are sterile. Turner's syndrome is caused by the absence of one X chromosome, giving \(45\) with \(XO\); such females are sterile with rudimentary ovaries and lack of secondary sexual characters.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Klinefelter's syndrome is \(47, XXY\) with gynaecomastia, and Turner's syndrome is \(45, XO\) with rudimentary ovaries.

answer.text: \(47, XXY\); furrowed tongue; \(45, XO\); broad palm crease

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q35 - Number of gamete types for four heterozygous loci

questiontext.text: A diploid organism is heterozygous for \(4\) independently assorting loci. How many genetically different types of gametes can it produce?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The organism is diploid and heterozygous at \(n = 4\) independently assorting loci (for example, \(AaBbCcDd\)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The four loci assort independently during meiosis without linkage.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment, the number of different gamete types is given by \(2^n\), where \(n\) is the number of heterozygous loci.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substituting \(n = 4\) into the formula gives \(2^4 = 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 16\) types of gametes.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Each locus contributes \(2\) allelic choices independently, so \(16\) distinct gamete genotypes are formed. The final answer is \(16\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q36 - Progeny phenotype proportions in TtYy x Ttyy cross

questiontext.text: When a cross is made between a tall plant with yellow seeds (\(TtYy\)) and a tall plant with green seeds (\(Ttyy\)), what proportions of phenotypes in the offspring are expected to be (i) tall and green, and (ii) dwarf and green, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Parental genotypes are \(TtYy\) (tall, yellow) and \(Ttyy\) (tall, green).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
\(T\) (tall) is dominant over \(t\) (dwarf), and \(Y\) (yellow) is dominant over \(y\) (green). Both loci assort independently.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Because the two genes assort independently, the combined phenotypic probability is the product of the individual probabilities from \(Tt \times Tt\) and \(Yy \times yy\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
From \(Tt \times Tt\), the probability of tall (\(TT\) or \(Tt\)) is \(\frac{3}{4}\) and of dwarf (\(tt\)) is \(\frac{1}{4}\). From \(Yy \times yy\), the probability of yellow (\(Yy\)) is \(\frac{1}{2}\) and of green (\(yy\)) is \(\frac{1}{2}\). Therefore:
(i) Proportion of tall and green \(= \frac{3}{4} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{3}{8}\).
(ii) Proportion of dwarf and green \(= \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{8}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking the remaining classes: tall and yellow \(= \frac{3}{8}\), dwarf and yellow \(= \frac{1}{8}\); total \(= \frac{3}{8} + \frac{1}{8} + \frac{3}{8} + \frac{1}{8} = 1\). The expected proportions are \(\frac{3}{8}\) and \(\frac{1}{8}\), respectively.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q37 - ABO blood group genotypes and offspring probabilities

questiontext.text: A child has blood group O. If the father has blood group A and the mother has blood group B, what are the genotypes of the parents and the probability that their next child will have blood group AB?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Father has blood group A, mother has blood group B, and one child has blood group O.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Blood group O has genotype \(ii\). Both \(I^A\) and \(I^B\) are completely dominant over \(i\) and co-dominant with each other.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For a child to inherit \(ii\), each parent must contribute one \(i\) allele.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since the father is blood group A and must carry an \(i\) allele, his genotype is \(I^A i\). Since the mother is blood group B and must carry an \(i\) allele, her genotype is \(I^B i\). Crossing \(I^A i \times I^B i\) yields four equally likely genotypes: \(I^A I^B\) (AB), \(I^A i\) (A), \(I^B i\) (B), and \(ii\) (O). Thus, the probability of an \(I^A I^B\) (blood group AB) child is \(\frac{1}{4}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
All four phenotypes (A, B, AB, O) appear with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\) each, summing to \(1\). The parental genotypes are \(I^A i\) and \(I^B i\), and the probability of blood group AB is \(\frac{1}{4}\).

answer.text: Father \(I^A i\), Mother \(I^B i\); probability of AB \(= \frac{1}{4}\)
Father \(I^A I^A\), Mother \(I^B i\); probability of AB \(= \frac{1}{2}\)
Father \(I^A i\), Mother \(I^B I^B\); probability of AB \(= \frac{1}{4}\)
Father \(I^A i\), Mother \(I^B i\); probability of AB \(= \frac{1}{2}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q38 - F1 phenotype in homozygous female by heterozygous male cross

questiontext.text: A cross is performed between a homozygous female and a heterozygous male for a single Mendelian locus (\(T/t\), where \(T\) is completely dominant over \(t\)). What will be the phenotypic distribution in the \(F_1\) generation if the female is (i) homozygous dominant, and (ii) homozygous recessive?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The male parent is heterozygous (\(Tt\)), producing \(50\%\,T\) and \(50\%\,t\) gametes. The female parent is homozygous, either \(TT\) or \(tt\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
\(T\) is completely dominant over \(t\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
A homozygous parent produces only one type of gamete.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Case (i): Crossing \(TT\text{ (female)} \times Tt\text{ (male)}\) yields \(50\%\,TT\) and \(50\%\,Tt\), so \(100\%\) of the \(F_1\) progeny express the dominant phenotype.
Case (ii): Crossing \(tt\text{ (female)} \times Tt\text{ (male)}\) yields \(50\%\,Tt\) (dominant phenotype) and \(50\%\,tt\) (recessive phenotype), giving a \(1:1\) phenotypic ratio.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
In Case (i) all progeny are dominant, and in Case (ii) half are dominant and half are recessive. Thus, the distributions are \(100\%\) dominant in (i) and \(1:1\) dominant to recessive in (ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q39 - Phenotypic ratio when two heterozygous loci are completely linked

questiontext.text: Two parents heterozygous for two dominant traits (\(AB/ab\), where the dominant alleles \(A\) and \(B\) are in cis configuration on one chromosome and \(a\) and \(b\) are on the homologous chromosome) are crossed. If the two loci are completely linked with zero recombination, what phenotypic ratio is expected in the offspring?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Both parents have genotype \(AB/ab\), and the two loci are completely linked (\(0\%\) recombination).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
\(A\) is dominant over \(a\) and \(B\) is dominant over \(b\). With zero recombination, no \(Ab\) or \(aB\) gametes are formed.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Completely linked genes segregate together as a single unit during meiosis, behaving like a single monohybrid locus.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Each parent produces only two types of gametes in equal proportions: \(50\%\,AB\) and \(50\%\,ab\). Random fertilisation yields \(\frac{1}{4}\,(AB/AB) : \frac{1}{2}\,(AB/ab) : \frac{1}{4}\,(ab/ab)\). Since both \(AB/AB\) and \(AB/ab\) express both dominant traits, \(\frac{3}{4}\) show the double-dominant phenotype and \(\frac{1}{4}\) show the double-recessive phenotype.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
No recombinant phenotypes appear. The expected phenotypic ratio is \(3:1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q40 - Cytological basis of independent assortment during Meiosis I

questiontext.text: Which cytological event during meiosis provides the physical basis for Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Independent assortment requires that different pairs of homologous chromosomes align and separate independently of one another during meiosis.

Step 2: Evaluation
During Anaphase of Meiosis I (following independent alignment of bivalents at the metaphase plate), the two non-homologous chromosome pairs can segregate to the poles in either combination (e.g., long orange with short green, or long orange with short red). This random orientation and separation at Meiosis I produces all four possible gamete combinations in equal frequencies.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Independent alignment and separation of non-homologous chromosome pairs during Anaphase of Meiosis I is the physical basis of independent assortment.

answer.text: Replication of DNA during the \(S\) phase before mitosis
Independent alignment and separation of different chromosome pairs during Anaphase of Meiosis I
Tight linkage of two genes located adjacent to each other on the same chromatid

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q41 - Offspring probability in polygenic skin colour cross

questiontext.text: Assuming human skin colour is controlled by three independently assorting genes (\(A, B, C\)) with additive effects, if two individuals with genotype \(AaBbCc\) marry, what fraction of their children is expected to have the darkest skin colour (\(AABBCC\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Both parents have genotype \(AaBbCc\) for three independently assorting polygenic loci.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Dominant alleles \(A, B, C\) contribute additively to dark skin colour, so \(AABBCC\) is the darkest phenotype.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For independent loci, the probability of a multi-locus genotype is the product of the probabilities at each individual locus.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
From \(Aa \times Aa\), the probability of \(AA\) is \(\frac{1}{4}\). Similarly, from \(Bb \times Bb\) the probability of \(BB\) is \(\frac{1}{4}\), and from \(Cc \times Cc\) the probability of \(CC\) is \(\frac{1}{4}\). Multiplying these probabilities gives:
\(P(AABBCC) = \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{64}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
With \(8\) gamete types per parent, there are \(8 \times 8 = 64\) combinations, of which exactly \(1\) is \(AABBCC\). The final answer is \(\frac{1}{64}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q42 - Incomplete dominance cross between pink and white snapdragons

questiontext.text: In Antirrhinum sp. (snapdragon), if a pink-flowered plant (\(Rr\)) is crossed with a white-flowered plant (\(rr\)), what phenotypic ratio is expected in the progeny?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
A pink-flowered snapdragon (\(Rr\)) is crossed with a white-flowered snapdragon (\(rr\)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Flower colour in snapdragon shows incomplete dominance: \(RR\) is red, \(Rr\) is pink, and \(rr\) is white.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
During meiosis, \(Rr\) produces \(50\%\,R\) and \(50\%\,r\) gametes, while \(rr\) produces \(100\%\,r\) gametes.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Combining the gametes gives \(50\%\,Rr\) (pink) and \(50\%\,rr\) (white), which is a \(1:1\) ratio of pink to white.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
No \(RR\) (red) plants can be formed because the \(rr\) parent lacks the \(R\) allele. The expected phenotypic ratio is \(1\text{ pink} : 1\text{ white}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q43 - Carrier probability and molecular defect in sickle-cell anaemia

questiontext.text: Two parents who are apparently unaffected carriers for sickle-cell anaemia (\(Hb^A Hb^S \times Hb^A Hb^S\)) have a child. What is the probability that the child is a carrier (exhibiting sickle-cell trait), and what is the underlying codon change in the \(\beta\)-globin gene?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Both parents are heterozygous carriers with genotype \(Hb^A Hb^S\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
\(Hb^A Hb^A\) is normal, \(Hb^A Hb^S\) is an apparently unaffected carrier (sickle-cell trait), and \(Hb^S Hb^S\) shows the diseased phenotype.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Mendelian segregation, \(Hb^A Hb^S \times Hb^A Hb^S\) produces \(\frac{1}{4}\,Hb^A Hb^A : \frac{1}{2}\,Hb^A Hb^S : \frac{1}{4}\,Hb^S Hb^S\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
The probability of the child having genotype \(Hb^A Hb^S\) (carrier) is \(\frac{1}{2}\) or \(50\%\). At the molecular level, sickle-cell anaemia results from a single base substitution at the sixth codon of the \(\beta\)-globin gene from \(\text{GAG}\) to \(\text{GUG}\), replacing Glutamic acid with Valine.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The carrier probability is \(50\%\), and the codon change is \(\text{GAG}\) to \(\text{GUG}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q44 - Distinguishing thalassemia from sickle-cell anaemia

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements accurately differentiates thalassemia from sickle-cell anaemia?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Both thalassemia and sickle-cell anaemia are autosomal recessive haemoglobinopathies, but they differ in whether the defect affects the quantity or the functional quality of globin chains.

Step 2: Evaluation
Thalassemia is a quantitative problem of synthesising too few \(\alpha\) or \(\beta\) globin molecules (due to mutation or deletion in \(HBA1/HBA2\) on chromosome \(16\) for \(\alpha\)-thalassemia, or \(HBB\) on chromosome \(11\) for \(\beta\)-thalassemia). By contrast, sickle-cell anaemia is a qualitative problem of synthesising an incorrectly functioning \(\beta\)-globin chain.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thalassemia is a quantitative problem of synthesising too few globin molecules, whereas sickle-cell anaemia is a qualitative problem of synthesising an incorrectly functioning globin.

answer.text: Thalassemia is a qualitative globin defect, whereas sickle-cell anaemia is a quantitative globin defect
Thalassemia is an X-linked recessive disorder, whereas sickle-cell anaemia is autosomal dominant
Thalassemia is a quantitative problem of synthesising too few globin molecules, whereas sickle-cell anaemia is a qualitative problem
\(\alpha\)-thalassemia is controlled by \(HBB\) on chromosome \(11\), whereas \(\beta\)-thalassemia is controlled by \(HBA1\) on chromosome \(16\)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q45 - Colour-blind daughter probability from carrier mother and affected father

questiontext.text: A woman with normal vision whose father was colour blind (making her a carrier, \(X^C X^c\)) marries a colour-blind man (\(X^c Y\)). What percentage of their daughters are expected to be colour blind?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mother is a carrier (\(X^C X^c\)) and father is colour blind (\(X^c Y\)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
\(X^C\) is the normal dominant allele and \(X^c\) is the recessive allele for red-green colour blindness.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Daughters inherit one X chromosome from the father and one X chromosome from the mother.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
The father (\(X^c Y\)) transmits \(X^c\) to all his daughters. The mother (\(X^C X^c\)) transmits \(X^C\) to \(50\%\) of her daughters (giving \(X^C X^c\), normal carrier) and \(X^c\) to \(50\%\) of her daughters (giving \(X^c X^c\), colour blind).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Among the daughters specifically, half are \(X^C X^c\) and half are \(X^c X^c\). Thus, \(50\%\) of their daughters are expected to be colour blind.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q46 - Pedigree logic ruling out X-linked recessive inheritance

questiontext.text: In a human family pedigree, two phenotypically normal parents have an affected daughter. Which mode of inheritance can be definitively ruled out?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Pedigree analysis uses parental and offspring phenotypes to eliminate incompatible modes of inheritance.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because both parents are unaffected and have an affected child, the trait must be recessive (so dominant traits are ruled out). If the trait were X-linked recessive, an affected daughter (\(X^a X^a\)) would have to inherit an \(X^a\) chromosome from her father, which would make the father affected (\(X^a Y\)). Since the father is phenotypically normal, X-linked recessive inheritance is ruled out, leaving autosomal recessive inheritance.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
X-linked recessive inheritance (as well as dominant inheritance) is ruled out; specifically, among recessive modes, X-linked recessive inheritance is definitively excluded.

answer.text: Both autosomal recessive and X-linked recessive inheritance

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q47 - Mechanism of aneuploidy versus polyploidy

questiontext.text: Failure of segregation of chromatids during the cell division cycle results in ______, whereas failure of cytokinesis after the telophase stage of cell division results in ______.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chromosomal number changes occur either at the level of individual chromosomes or at the level of entire chromosome sets.

Step 2: Evaluation
Failure of chromatid segregation during cell division leads to the gain or loss of one or more individual chromosomes, a condition called aneuploidy (e.g., Down's syndrome and Turner's syndrome). Failure of cytokinesis after telophase results in an increase in a whole set of chromosomes, known as polyploidy (commonly seen in plants).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The two conditions in order are aneuploidy and polyploidy.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER5_MCQ_Q48 - Generational inheritance in haplodiploid honey bee males

questiontext.text: Why can a male honey bee (drone) have a grandfather and grandsons, even though it cannot have a father or sons?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the haplodiploid system of honey bees, sex is determined by the number of chromosome sets: fertilised eggs become diploid females (\(32\)), and unfertilised eggs become haploid males (\(16\)) by parthenogenesis.

Step 2: Evaluation
A drone develops from an unfertilised egg of a queen, so he has no father. However, his mother (the queen) developed from a fertilised egg and therefore has a father—the drone's maternal grandfather. Similarly, when the drone produces sperm by mitosis and fertilises a queen's egg, the resulting offspring is a diploid daughter (queen or worker), not a son; that daughter can then produce unfertilised eggs that develop into the drone's grandsons.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A drone develops parthenogenetically from an unfertilised egg (no father), and his sperm fertilising an egg produces only daughters, who can then bear his grandsons parthenogenetically.

answer.text: Drones develop from fertilised eggs and transmit only their Y chromosome to daughters
Drones arise from unfertilised eggs of a diploid mother (who has a father) and their sperm only produce daughters, who can bear grandsons
Drones undergo meiosis to produce diploid sperm that fertilise eggs to form grandsons directly
Drones are sterile and inherit chromosomes only from worker bees
